analysis.one_liner: Gives internet users the right to see, control, and limit how companies collect their personal data.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan online privacy bill introduced in April 2018 never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Commerce Committee and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required websites, apps, social networks, and other online platforms to tell users up front that their personal data will be collected and used, and to let users opt out. It would have given users the right to a free copy of the data a company keeps on them, a list of who that data was sold to, notice within 72 hours when their data was misused, and the option to have their data erased. It would have let the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general enforce these rules, including against internet providers and nonprofits that are currently outside the FTC's reach.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users — essentially everyone who uses social media, search engines, email, mobile apps, or internet service — would gain real control over how their personal data is collected, sold, and used. Today most people have no practical way to see what data a company holds on them or who it has been sold to.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Internet users, especially social media and app users

how_it_helps.text: Before a user creates an account or begins using a platform, the operator must disclose that the user's personal data will be collected and used by the operator and third parties, and must offer the user the option to prohibit that collection [S2] [S3].
Operators must offer users a free, electronic copy of all personal data the company has processed on them, including a list of every person the data was sold or otherwise transferred to [S2] [S3].

When a user's data has been transmitted in violation of the company's privacy or security program, the operator must notify the user within 72 hours and offer options to erase the data, stop its further dissemination, and close the account [S2] [S3].

Violations would count as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act, and the bill extends FTC enforcement to common carriers (like internet providers) and nonprofits that are currently exempt or largely exempt from FTC authority; state attorneys general could also sue in federal court [S2] [S3].
Users could withdraw consent to data collection as easily as they gave it, and no one could access a user's personal data more than 30 days after the user closes an account [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Online platforms — social networks, search engines, ad networks, mobile operating systems, email services, and internet providers — would bear compliance costs and, more significantly, would lose the ability to freely collect and monetize users' behavioral data, which underpins much of the online advertising business.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tech platforms, ad networks, and data brokers

drawbacks.text: The bill lets an operator deny a user certain services or completely deny access if the user's opt-out of data collection 'creates inoperability in the platform' — a broad exception that could let companies present users with a choice between full data collection and losing the service [S2] [S3].
The bill provides no right for individuals to sue on their own; enforcement rests entirely with the FTC and state attorneys general, so wronged users would depend on government action [S2] [S3].

The 72-hour notice duty applies when data is 'transmitted in violation of the privacy or security program,' a narrower trigger than standard data-breach notification laws covering any breach of data the company holds [S3].
Subsections on disclosure, access, and misuse do not apply to an operator's development of privacy-enhancing technology, a carve-out that could shelter substantial data work from the rules [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — disclosure, opt-out rights, data access, a list of who your data was sold to, and 72-hour misuse notice — would have given ordinary users protections they do not have today. But the design has real weaknesses: the inoperability exception could blunt the opt-out right at the biggest platforms, individuals could not sue on their own, and the misuse-notice trigger is narrow. A stronger bill would close the service-denial loophole and add a private right of action.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in April 2018, and the committee never held a hearing, markup, or floor vote on it before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on April 23, 2018, joined by Senator John Kennedy, giving it one Republican cosponsor [S1] [S4] [S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on April 23, 2018 [S2] [S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it never reached the Senate floor before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online platforms, ad networks, and data brokers kept collecting and selling users' personal data without the disclosure, opt-out, and access rights this bill would have imposed. Users gained nothing; their data remained theirs to give away unknowingly.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tech platforms and data brokers kept their data profits

industries.industry: Online platforms and digital advertising (social networks, search engines, ad networks)
industries.note: Their business depends on collecting users' behavioral data and using or selling it for targeted advertising. The bill's disclosure and opt-out rights, plus a required list of every recipient of a user's data, would directly constrain that model, though the inoperability exception lets them deny service to users who opt out.

The bill would have forced operators to disclose to users a list of every person who received their personal data through sale or other means, and to stop access within 30 days of account closure, cutting into brokers' supply of sellable data.

Common carriers are currently exempt from FTC enforcement; the bill would have made them subject to the same privacy rules as every other platform, removing a regulatory advantage they hold over other data collectors.
